title: Severe COVID-19 reactivates dormant viruses and may leave a lasting viral signature - News-Medical

analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-07; study period May 2020–March 2021; longitudinal follow-up up to 12 months post-hospitalization (N12, N17).
analysis.location_and_population: United States; 1,154 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in the IMPACC cohort; no prior COVID-19 vaccination (N12, N15).
analysis.event: A Nature study reports SARS-CoV-2 infection can reactivate dormant chronic viruses (Anelloviridae, Herpesviridae) in immunocompetent individuals, with persistent Anelloviridae activity linked to long COVID physical deficits; findings challenge the view that reactivation occurs mainly in immunosuppressed patients (N3, N4, N44).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 1,154 hospitalized COVID-19 patients analyzed; viral reactivation detected across compartments; Anelloviridae and EBV transcripts associated with increased one-year mortality in critically ill subgroup; Anelloviridae counts higher in older adults and those with prior transplantation, myocardial infarction, shock, ICU admission, or immunosuppression (N12, N31, N32).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Longitudinal multi-omics profiling (RNA-seq, CyTOF, PEA, MS) identified temporal patterns of reactivation; external cohort reproduced patterns; authors propose qPCR monitoring but note no established clinical protocols; immunological consequences remain incompletely understood (N16, N18, N27, N47, N9).

analysis.brief_en: A Nature study of 1,154 unvaccinated U.S. patients hospitalized for COVID-19 between May 2020 and March 2021 reports that severe SARS-CoV-2 infection can reactivate dormant chronic viruses—including Anelloviridae and Herpesviridae—in people without overt immunosuppression. Persistent Anelloviridae activity during convalescence correlated with long COVID characterized by physical deficits, and viral reactivation patterns tracked disease severity. Critically ill patients with cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, or herpes simplex virus transcripts had higher one-year mortality, while Anelloviridae loads were elevated in older adults and those with prior organ transplant, myocardial infarction, shock, ICU care, or immunosuppression. The authors suggest quantitative PCR monitoring could aid prognostication, but emphasize that standardized clinical protocols and a full understanding of immune consequences are still lacking.
